questions.q: Why does this lesson say a vague professional-summary line underperforms a specific skills line on a ServiceNow-track resume?
options: Because recruiters and ATS keyword matching respond far more reliably to named platform capabilities than to adjectives
Because professional summaries are never read by anyone
Because ServiceNow resumes are not scanned by applicant tracking systems
Because specific skills lines are required by ServiceNow's certification program
questions.explain: Named modules, scripting constructs, and integration tools match what a recruiter or an ATS is actually scanning for; summary adjectives don't.

questions.q: What does a well-built resume bullet, as described in this lesson, actually consist of?
options: A list of every lesson covered in the relevant course
What was built, the specific ServiceNow capability it demonstrates, and the outcome stated in defensible terms
A restatement of the job posting's exact language
A single adjective describing the candidate's work ethic
questions.explain: Each bullet should translate one real artifact into capability-plus-outcome language, built from the actual project work.

questions.q: Why does this lesson caution against a claim like "reduced ticket resolution time by 40%" for a course lab project?
options: Because percentages are never appropriate on any resume
Because these are lab/capstone projects on a PDI with no real user population or baseline to measure against, so the number can't be backed up
Because ServiceNow prohibits mentioning metrics in job applications
Because interviewers never ask how a number was measured
questions.explain: Without a real baseline or real users, a specific percentage is an invented number that a good interviewer will ask you to defend — and you can't.

questions.q: What is a "structural claim," as this lesson uses the term, and why does it recommend one instead of an invented percentage?
options: A claim about the building's physical structure where the work was performed
A specific, honest statement about what changed (e.g., manual process became automated) without an unverifiable number
A claim that only architects are allowed to make on their resumes
A statement that avoids naming any ServiceNow capability at all
questions.explain: A structural claim like "automated a manual, multi-step routing process" is true and specific without requiring a number you can't support.

questions.q: How should an in-progress certification like CSA be listed on a resume, per this lesson?
options: Listed exactly as "ServiceNow Certified System Administrator" with no qualifier, even if the exam hasn't been passed
Left off the resume entirely until it's fully earned
Labeled clearly as in progress, such as "CSA — in progress," so the recruiter knows exactly where you stand
Listed as earned, since studying for it demonstrates the same skill as passing it
questions.explain: Implying an unearned certification is already held is the kind of claim that gets caught and costs more credibility than honestly labeling it in progress.
